name: alist-delete
summary: A new association list with EVERY pair whose key matches removed, not just the first.
explanation: alist-delete is the counterweight to alist-cons. Where alist-cons pushes a pair on the front and leaves everything underneath, alist-delete sweeps the whole list and drops every entry whose key matches -- all of them, not the first one, which is the single most important thing to know about it. That is deliberate: an alist built by pushing can accumulate several pairs for one key, and deleting only the front one would uncover a stale value that the caller thought was gone. Sweeping is the only behaviour that makes 'this key is now absent' true. The comparison defaults to equal?, not eq?, so string and list keys work without saying anything, and you pass a third argument only when you want something narrower or looser. The result is always a fresh list -- the original is untouched -- and a key that was never present costs a full traversal and returns a copy, so alist-delete is never free even when it does nothing.

examples.note: ((a . 1) (c . 3)) -- b is gone, the order of the rest is preserved.
(all-gone ((y . 2)) original ((x . 3) (y . 2) (x . 1)) absent ((x . 3) (y . 2) (x . 1))) -- BOTH x pairs go, the source is untouched, and deleting a missing key just gives the list back.

examples.code:
(define (set-key key value alist)
  (alist-cons key value (alist-delete key alist)))
(define a (set-key 'a 9 (set-key 'a 1 (set-key 'b 2 '()))))
(display (list 'alist a 'length (length a) 'a (cdr (assq 'a a))))
(newline)
examples.note: (alist ((a . 9) (b . 2)) length 2 a 9) -- delete-then-cons is the replacing update. Without the delete, length would be 3.

caveats: It removes EVERY match, not the first. That is the difference from popping a scope frame; if you wanted only the front pair gone, use cdr.
The default comparison is equal?, not eq?. String keys work with no third argument, which is convenient and is the opposite of what assq does -- do not assume the two agree.
It always returns a fresh list and always traverses the whole thing, even when the key is absent. There is no early exit and no sharing of the untouched tail.
The optional comparison procedure is called with the KEY first and the alist entry's key second. A non-symmetric comparison will behave differently from the order you might expect.
It is not the update operator. (alist-delete k a) then (alist-cons k v ...) is the replace idiom; using delete alone leaves the key absent, and using cons alone leaves the old pair buried.
usecases: Replacing a key's value for real, by deleting then consing, so the list does not grow on every update.
Clearing a setting so that a lower-priority default underneath becomes visible again.
Trimming an alist built by pushing before handing it to something that iterates rather than looks up.

learn.concept: Deleting every match rather than the first is what makes absence mean absence, and it is why delete-then-cons is the honest way to update an association list.
learn.progression: Delete a key that appears once and it is unremarkable. Delete a key that appears twice, count what is left, and the design choice becomes visible. Then write delete-then-cons and notice you have re-derived what a mutable dictionary does in one step -- and what it costs in a list.

row-2-audit.eng-program:
(define (clear-override key settings) (alist-delete key settings))
(define layered '((volume . 9) (theme . dark) (volume . 5) (theme . light) (lang . en)))
(define reset (clear-override 'volume layered))
(display (list 'remaining (map car reset)
               'theme (cdr (assq 'theme reset))
               'volume (assq 'volume reset)))
(newline)
row-2-audit.math-program:
(define (restrict-away x f) (alist-delete x f))
(define f '((1 . 1) (2 . 4) (3 . 9) (4 . 16)))
(display (list 'domain (map car (restrict-away 3 f))
               'size (length (restrict-away 3 f))
               'absent-noop (length (restrict-away 99 f))))
(newline)
row-2-audit.problem: A settings stack has accumulated three overrides of one key and the operator wants that key genuinely reset to nothing. Candidates: alist-delete (sweeps every matching pair in one pass, which is exactly 'reset'), cdr (removes only the newest override and silently promotes the second-newest, which looks like it worked), filter with a lambda comparing car (identical behaviour, and it is what alist-delete is, but written out and easy to get the sense backwards), remove from SRFI-1 (same shape, operates on the whole pair rather than the key, so the lambda has to do the car itself), a hash table delete (right answer if the structure were a hash table, but it is not and converting costs more than the sweep). alist-delete wins because the requirement is total absence, and only a sweep gives that.
row-2-audit.explanation: eng: clearing an override from a layered settings list, showing that BOTH volume pairs went and that assq now answers #f. math: the same call read as restricting a finite map by removing a point from its domain, including the no-op case where the point was never in the domain. cs: the three traps side by side -- delete-all versus cdr, a string key working under the default equal?, and the SAME string key surviving when eq? is forced.
row-2-audit.meta: Why alist-delete and not cdr: cdr is O(1) and looks correct on a list where the key appears once. It is wrong on exactly the lists that alist-cons produces, which is the only kind of list anyone would be deleting from.
row-2-audit.eng: 'Reset to default' means every layer of override is gone. Removing one layer leaves a value the user already replaced once and thought they were rid of.
row-2-audit.math: Restricting a function's domain by removing a point is total: it is defined whether or not the point was in the domain, and it never fails.
row-2-audit.cs: The equal?-by-default choice is the trap. alist-delete finds string keys that assq cannot, so a program that stores with assq and clears with alist-delete has two different notions of the same key.

row-3-dimension.setup: Removing everything filed under one label, and having 'removed' mean there is nothing left underneath.

rungs.domain: decommissioning a sensor and purging every reading it filed, in degrees Celsius
rungs.code:
(define readings '((roof . 21) (cellar . 12) (roof . 19) (yard . 15) (roof . 22)))
(define (decommission station log) (alist-delete station log))
(define left (decommission 'roof readings))
(display (list 'stations (map car left)
               'mean-left (/ (apply + (map cdr left)) (length left))
               'purged (- (length readings) (length left))))
(newline)

rungs.domain: cache invalidation: an entry and every stale generation of it must go together
rungs.code:
(define cache '((page-1 . v3) (page-2 . v1) (page-1 . v2) (page-1 . v1)))
(define (invalidate key entries) (alist-delete key entries))
(define (hit? key entries) (if (assq key entries) 'hit 'miss))
(define after (invalidate 'page-1 cache))
(display (list 'before (hit? 'page-1 cache)
               'after (hit? 'page-1 after)
               'others (hit? 'page-2 after)
               'entries-left (length after)))
(newline)

row-3-dimension.explanation: Bare, it is a filter with three outcomes worth seeing: one match removed, two matches removed, and no match removed. On a log of measurements it becomes decommissioning -- a station goes away and every reading it ever filed goes with it, which changes the mean of what remains, so the deletion is not merely cosmetic. As cache invalidation it becomes a correctness requirement: leaving one stale generation behind means the next lookup returns an old version, and the bug is a wrong answer rather than a slow one. Same call each time; what climbs is the cost of doing it only partially -- from nothing, to a skewed average, to serving stale data.
row-3-dimension.meta: The rungs are ordered by what a PARTIAL delete would cost. That is the honest ladder for this verb, because sweeping-versus-popping is its only real design decision and its consequences only become visible when there is something underneath.
row-3-dimension.eng: Purging a source means purging its history too, or every statistic computed afterwards is quietly wrong.
row-3-dimension.math: Removing a point from a domain changes every aggregate over that domain. The mean of the remainder is not the mean of the whole minus something -- it has to be recomputed.
row-3-dimension.cs: Cache invalidation that leaves a shadowed older entry is worse than no invalidation, because the miss path was correct and the stale hit is not.

row-4-proof.eng-program:
(define (key-is-gone? k al)
  (not (assoc k (alist-delete k al))))
(display (map (lambda (al) (key-is-gone? 'x al))
              '(((x . 1)) ((x . 1) (x . 2)) ((a . 1) (x . 2) (b . 3) (x . 4)) () ((a . 1)))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.math-program:
(define (removes-exactly-the-matches? k al)
  (= (length (alist-delete k al))
     (length (filter (lambda (p) (not (equal? (car p) k))) al))))
(display (map (lambda (al) (removes-exactly-the-matches? 'x al))
              '(((x . 1) (y . 2)) ((x . 1) (x . 2) (x . 3)) ((y . 1) (z . 2)) () ((x . 1)))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.cs-program:
(define (order-of-survivors-kept? k al)
  (equal? (map car (alist-delete k al))
          (remove (lambda (c) (equal? c k)) (map car al))))
(display (map (lambda (al) (order-of-survivors-kept? 'x al))
              '(((a . 1) (x . 2) (b . 3)) ((x . 1) (a . 2) (x . 3) (b . 4)) ((a . 1) (b . 2)) ((x . 1)) ())))
(newline)
row-4-proof.claim: After deleting a key it can never be found again; the number of pairs removed is exactly the number that matched, no more and no fewer; and the pairs that survive keep their original relative order.
row-4-proof.invariant: For all keys k and alists a. assoc(k, alist-delete(k, a)) = #f; |alist-delete(k, a)| = |{p in a : car(p) != k}|; and map(car, alist-delete(k, a)) = the subsequence of map(car, a) with every k removed
row-4-proof.meta: Three claims because three distinct failures are possible: leaving a match behind (the shadowing bug), removing too much (a comparison that is too loose), and reordering the survivors (an implementation that rebuilt by consing without reversing). The multi-match lists are what separate a sweep from a pop; the empty list and the no-match list are where an implementation with an early exit would diverge.
row-4-proof.eng: 'Cannot be found afterwards' is the only property a caller actually depends on. Everything else about the verb is an implementation detail.
row-4-proof.math: The count law states that delete is exactly a filter -- it removes the preimage of k under car and nothing else, so the operation is determined entirely by the comparison.
row-4-proof.cs: Order preservation is not free. It is the difference between a fold that conses and one that conses then reverses, and it matters because assq's answer depends on order.

row-5-emergence.eng-composition:
(define (clear key settings) (alist-delete key settings))
(define (set-setting key value settings)
  (alist-cons key value (clear key settings)))
(define (apply-edits edits settings)
  (fold (lambda (e acc) (set-setting (car e) (cdr e) acc)) settings edits))
(define final (apply-edits '((volume . 9) (theme . dark) (volume . 11))
                           '((volume . 5) (theme . light) (lang . en))))
(display (list 'settings (map car final) 'volume (cdr (assq 'volume final)) 'size (length final)))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.math-composition:
(define (drop-point x f) (alist-delete x f))
(define (restrict-to xs f)
  (fold (lambda (x acc) (if (member x xs) acc (drop-point x acc))) f (map car f)))
(define squares '((1 . 1) (2 . 4) (3 . 9) (4 . 16) (5 . 25)))
(display (list 'evens (restrict-to '(2 4) squares)
               'none (restrict-to '() squares)
               'all (length (restrict-to '(1 2 3 4 5) squares))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.cs-composition:
(define (evict key entries) (alist-delete key entries))
(define (compact entries)
  (fold (lambda (p acc)
          (if (assq (car p) acc) acc (append acc (list p))))
        '() entries))
(define (evict-then-compact key entries) (compact (evict key entries)))
(define cache '((a . v3) (b . v1) (a . v2) (c . v1) (b . v0) (a . v1)))
(display (list 'raw (length cache)
               'compacted (map car (compact cache))
               'after-evict (evict-then-compact 'a cache)))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.base: alist-delete removes every pair filed under one key and gives back a fresh list.
row-5-emergence.emergent: eng: clear is one call; set-setting pairs it with alist-cons to make a REPLACING update, and apply-edits folds that over a batch -- so three edits including a repeat of the same key leave a list that is still exactly three long. Growth is eliminated by the composition, not by the verb. math: drop-point is one call; restrict-to folds it over the keys NOT wanted, which turns a removal into a selection -- the same operation read from the other side. cs: evict is one call; compact keeps only the newest generation of each key, and composing the two gives a cache maintenance pass where eviction and compaction are separately testable.
row-5-emergence.meta: The pattern in all three is delete-under-a-fold, and what varies is what the fold is folding over: the edits, the unwanted keys, or the entries themselves. The first is the one worth internalising, because delete-then-cons is the missing 'update' verb that neither alist-cons nor alist-delete is on its own.
row-5-emergence.eng: An update built from delete-then-cons keeps the list bounded by the number of distinct keys, which is the property that makes an alist usable for long-lived state at all.
row-5-emergence.math: Restricting a domain to a set is the complement of removing points one at a time. Writing it as a fold over the unwanted keys makes the two views literally the same code.
row-5-emergence.cs: Separating evict from compact means the eviction policy can change without touching the compaction, and each can be proved on its own.
